title: Hex Siege
premise: A compact turn-based clan duel on a small hex board where both sides reposition stones to surround and collapse the opposing line.
interaction_model: Tap or click a friendly piece, view highlighted legal destinations, and tap a target hex to make a move in alternating turns against an AI opponent.
objective: Reduce the opposing Iron Clan to two stones or fewer by maneuvering pieces into surround formations while avoiding your own encirclement and obeying the no-three-allies-in-a-row rule.
progression: Single-match tactical escalation with no persistent meta layer: opening positioning, midgame surround threats, cascading captures, and a win/loss end screen with instant restart.
theme: Neon sci-fi flavored abstract board warfare framed as a Red Clan versus Iron Clan siege.
mood: Tense, readable, arcade-polished, and quick to replay.
likely_audience: players who enjoy abstract strategy games
casual tactics players looking for short sessions
confidence_notes: High confidence in the core rules, turn order, capture condition, and win state because they are directly encoded in the game logic.
High confidence that the game is intended for touch/mobile play due to fullscreen canvas input, safe-area CSS, and simple tap interactions.
Moderate confidence that the center-hex long movement is a deliberate signature rule, because it exists in move generation but is not surfaced in the visible rules text.
Low confidence in any broader narrative or progression beyond a single self-contained duel because no campaign, levels, or unlock systems are present.
recreation_prompt: Recreate a browser-based game called "Hex Siege," a fast turn-based abstract strategy duel on a radius-3 hexagonal board with a neon sci-fi clan-war presentation. The player controls the Red Clan and plays against an AI-controlled Iron Clan. Each side begins with 6 round token-like pieces placed on opposite edges of the hex board. On your turn, you click or tap one of your own pieces to highlight legal moves, then choose an empty destination hex. Most pieces can move exactly 1 hex in any of the 6 hex directions, but a piece standing on the exact center hex gains special sliding movement along straight hex lines until blocked or until the board edge. A move is illegal if it would leave 3 allied pieces aligned in a straight row, so move generation must enforce a strict no-three-in-a-row rule for the moving side. After every move, resolve captures simultaneously by checking every piece on the board: any piece that is adjacent to 3 or more enemy pieces is removed. This means both sides can lose pieces in the same resolution step. The match ends when either side is reduced to 2 pieces or fewer; if the AI falls to 2 or fewer the player wins, and if the player falls to 2 or fewer the player loses. Include a simple heuristic AI that evaluates all legal moves, strongly prefers moves that create captures, strongly avoids suicidal moves that would get itself surrounded, and mildly prefers central positioning. Present the game with a fullscreen canvas, glowing circular board sockets, glossy animated clan pieces, a HUD showing both remaining piece counts and whose turn it is, plus a start screen and restartable game-over screen. Use a touch-friendly click/tap interaction model, short toast messages for invalid actions, subtle movement animation, ambient music, UI/capture/win/lose sound effects, and celebratory or defeat GIF-style feedback overlays to give the abstract tactics a punchy arcade feel.
